items.stem: You are an analyst in the M&A team of a mid-sized investment bank. Last night you sent your associate a merger model that she will use to build pages for a client call tomorrow afternoon. This morning, reviewing the file, you realise that the synergies have been added twice in the pro forma EPS calculation, overstating accretion by about 4 percentage points. The associate has not yet started building the pages, and nobody else has seen the model. What should you do?
options: Correct the model, send the new version to the associate straight away and explain clearly what was wrong and which outputs change.
Correct the model and quietly replace the file on the shared drive, since she has not started using it yet.
Tell the associate there is an issue with the model and ask her how she would like you to handle it before changing anything.
Leave the model as it is for now, since she will review it anyway and is likely to spot the double count herself.

steps: A is the best (ownership, integrity): you fix it straight away, before the error reaches the client pages, and explain what has changed, so the associate can keep trusting your numbers.
D is the worst: you know there is an error and you leave it in the process hoping someone else will find it. If it slips through, an accretion overstated by 4 points ends up in front of the client.

B (2) fixes the technical problem but hides it: the associate might have a local copy or may already have seen the old numbers, and finding out later undermines trust. C (3) is transparent but slow: you hand the associate a decision that is yours to make, namely correcting your own work.
explanation.shortcut: Your own error, found before it does damage: fix it and immediately communicate what has changed.
explanation.trap: B looks efficient because 'nobody has used the file yet', but correcting silently is a transparency problem, not a technical one.
explanation.rule: Own your mistakes: correction and explicit communication, always together.

items.stem: You are a graduate in a corporate banking team. A week after a refinancing you worked on closes, the CFO of the client company sends you a parcel containing a luxury watch and a handwritten note thanking you for 'all the late nights'. You know the bank has a gifts and entertainment policy requiring gifts above a modest value to be declared and approved, but you have never read it in detail. Colleagues joke that 'everyone keeps these'. What should you do?
options: Keep the watch, since it was sent to you personally and the deal has already closed.
Read the gifts policy, declare the watch to compliance straight away and follow their guidance on keeping or returning it.
Return the watch to the CFO with a polite thank-you note explaining that you cannot accept it, without telling anyone at the bank.
Mention it to your manager and ask how gifts like this are normally handled in the team, before deciding what to do with it.

steps: B is the best (integrity): the policy exists precisely for cases like this. Declaring it immediately creates a record and leaves the decision to compliance, protecting you, the client and the bank.

A is the worst: a valuable gift from a client, left undeclared, is a potential conflict of interest even after the deal has closed, because the relationship continues. 'Everyone does it' is not a justification.

D (3) goes in the right direction because you ask a senior for guidance, but it stays informal and does not guarantee the required registration. C (2) reaches an ethically correct outcome but skips the declaration and decides alone on an issue that affects the client relationship.
explanation.shortcut: Valuable gift from a client: the best response almost always contains 'policy' and 'compliance'.
explanation.trap: Quietly returning it (C) looks like the most ethical choice, but in bank tests the process, i.e. declaring, matters as much as the outcome.
explanation.rule: When in doubt about gifts and benefits: declare first, then decide together with compliance.

items.stem: You are an analyst working on a confidential sell-side process for a listed software company. The deal is at an advanced stage and has not been announced. At dinner with university friends, one of them, who now works at a hedge fund, mentions a press rumour that the company is 'in play' and asks, half joking, whether your bank is involved and whether the rumour is true. Everyone at the table turns to look at you. What should you do?
options: Say, in a friendly but firm way, that you never comment on rumours or on the bank's clients, and change the subject.
Laugh it off and say, with a wink, that the rumour 'is not completely crazy', without giving any names or further details.
Say that your bank is not involved and that the rumour is probably wrong, to close the topic quickly before anyone asks more.
Excuse yourself from the table for a few minutes and, when you come back, steer the conversation onto a completely different topic.

steps: A is the best (integrity, communication): a neutral, standard phrase neither confirms nor denies, and it is what any banker says in these situations. The friendly tone avoids awkwardness.
B is the worst: telling someone who works at a hedge fund that the rumour is 'not entirely absurd' amounts to passing on inside information. It is a market abuse risk for you and for the bank.

C (2) reveals no details but is a lie, and an explicit denial becomes a signal once the deal is announced. D (3) avoids the leak but is clumsy: it does not set a clear boundary and the topic may come up again.
explanation.shortcut: On a confidential deal the right answer does not confirm, does not deny and does not lie.
explanation.trap: Denying (C) looks prudent, but it is still a statement about the deal, and a false one.
explanation.rule: Neither confirm nor deny: always use the same neutral phrase, with everyone.

items.stem: It is your first week on a graduate rotation in the rates sales team. A busy director stops by your desk, asks you to 'pull together the usual client pack on the curve moves' by 4 pm, and walks off into a meeting. You do not know what the usual pack looks like, which clients it is for or which maturities matter. Your desk neighbour, a second-year analyst, is on an internal call that should end in a few minutes. What should you do?
options: Start building a pack from scratch based on your own judgement of what the clients will want, to show the director that you can work independently.
Once your neighbour is off the call, ask for the previous version of the pack, start from it and message the director to confirm your understanding.
Email the director saying the request was too vague and that you will start once they explain exactly what is needed.
Wait for the director to come out of the meeting and ask them directly what the pack should contain, starting only once you have a clear answer.

steps: B is the best (communication, ownership): you use the nearest resource to find the standard format, start straight away and confirm your assumptions in writing, so the director can correct you in ten seconds between meetings.
C is the worst: the tone is accusatory towards a senior at your very first interaction, and you block the work instead of looking for a solution.

D (3) gives you reliable information but uses up precious time and depends on when the meeting ends. A (2) shows initiative but risks producing a useless pack, because 'the usual' points to a format that already exists.
explanation.shortcut: Vague instruction: first look for a precedent or a colleague, then confirm your assumptions with the person who asked for the work.
explanation.trap: A looks proactive, but independence without clarifying the format is just wasted time.
explanation.rule: Clarify early, with the right person, without stopping the work.

items.stem: You are at a bank's assessment centre, taking part in a 30-minute group case on whether a client should acquire a competitor. One candidate keeps talking over everyone and pushing his own conclusion. Another candidate has barely spoken, but at the start she made a sharp point about financing risk that nobody picked up. Twelve minutes are left and the group has not agreed a structure for the final presentation. What should you do?
options: Focus on preparing your own section of the presentation so that your individual contribution stands out to the assessors.
Tell the dominant candidate, in front of the group, that he is not letting anyone else speak.
Propose a quick structure for the remaining time and invite the quieter candidate to expand on her financing point.
Back the dominant candidate's conclusion to save time, but suggest the group lists the key risks together before finalising the slides.

steps: C is the best (teamwork, communication): you give the group what it lacks, namely structure and timing, and you bring back a valuable contribution that had gone unheard. This is the behaviour assessors look for.
B is the worst: publicly criticising another candidate creates conflict, wastes precious minutes and is read as a lack of maturity, even if the problem is real.

D (3) helps to reach a conclusion and puts the risks on the table, but accepts the dominant dynamic without giving the others space. A (2) ignores the group: in a group exercise an isolated individual contribution is worth little.
explanation.shortcut: In the group exercise the winner is whoever facilitates: structure, time and involving the others.
explanation.trap: A looks clever as a way to 'get noticed', but assessors evaluate how you work with others, not just what you say.
explanation.rule: Facilitate: do not dominate and do not isolate yourself.

items.stem: You are a first-year analyst in a corporate banking team. You spent two days on your first credit memo for a mid-cap client. Your VP returns it covered in comments, says the risk section 'reads like a company brochure' and that the cash-flow analysis ignores working-capital seasonality. You think some comments are harsh, and a couple concern points you believe you did cover. The memo is due at the credit committee in four days. What should you do?
options: Accept all the comments without discussion and rewrite the memo exactly as the VP suggests, so that the revised version is ready well before the committee.
Reply to the VP by email listing each comment you consider unfair, with page references showing where you had already covered the point.
Make the changes you agree with and leave the other sections unchanged, since you believe those points are already covered in the memo.
Ask the VP for 15 minutes to discuss the comments, clarify the points you believe you covered and agree what a strong risk section looks like.

steps: D is the best (resilience, communication): you treat the feedback as information, clarify constructively where you think you had already covered the point and ask for a concrete reference for the risks section. With four days of margin there is time to do it properly.
B is the worst: a point-by-point written reply on what is 'unfair' is defensive, irritates the VP and shifts the discussion from how to improve the memo to who is right.

A (3) is collaborative and quick, but you give up on understanding the VP's criteria and risk repeating the same mistake. C (2) silently ignores part of the feedback: if the VP does not see the changes, the memo comes back and trust falls.
explanation.shortcut: Tough feedback: listen, clarify in person, agree the standard, apply it.
explanation.trap: A looks like the humble answer, but without a conversation you do not find out what 'brochure' really means to that VP.
explanation.rule: Feedback is discussed in order to understand it, not to win the argument.

items.stem: You work for a global asset manager in London and are preparing a quarterly review for an institutional client. You need performance attribution data from a colleague in the Singapore office whom you have never met. You sent her a short message three days ago and have had no reply. The review is due to your portfolio manager on Friday, in two days, and your working hours overlap for only one hour each morning. What should you do?
options: Build the attribution yourself from the raw data using your own approach, even though you do not know the firm's methodology, and put it in the review.
Escalate to her manager in Singapore, explaining that she has not replied to your request and that your client deadline is now at risk.
Send her a specific request listing the exact data and the Friday deadline, and propose a 15-minute call in tomorrow's overlapping hour.
Tell your portfolio manager that the review may be late because the Singapore office has not replied to your request.

steps: C is the best (communication, teamwork): the first message was probably too generic. A precise request, with a deadline and a proposed call in the only overlapping hour, makes it easy for your colleague to help you.
A is the worst: building an attribution on your own with a methodology you do not know risks putting wrong numbers in front of an institutional client.

D (3) correctly manages the PM's expectations, but on its own solves nothing: it should be done in parallel with a concrete action. B (2) is a premature escalation after a single message and risks damaging the relationship with a colleague you will need every quarter.
explanation.shortcut: First make the request easy to fulfil, then escalate if necessary.
explanation.trap: B looks decisive, but going over someone's head after a single message is read as poor collaboration.
explanation.rule: In remote work: a specific request, a clear deadline, a synchronous channel when needed.

items.stem: You are a graduate in a corporate finance team. During a team lunch, a senior analyst imitates the accent of a new colleague from Nigeria while retelling something she said in a meeting, and a few people laugh. Your new colleague smiles but goes quiet for the rest of lunch, and later you notice she seems uncomfortable around the senior analyst. You are junior to him but get on well with him. What should you do?
options: Do nothing for now, since your colleague has not complained and you do not want to damage your relationship with the senior analyst.
Report the senior analyst's behaviour to HR straight away, without speaking to your colleague or to him first.
Tell your colleague it was only banter and that she will fit in better if she does not take that kind of joke personally.
Check in privately with your colleague, and tell the senior analyst one-to-one that the joke came across as hurtful.

steps: D is the best (integrity, teamwork): you support your colleague, understand how she experienced it and address the behaviour privately and directly with the person responsible. It is proportionate and is often enough to stop it happening again.
C is the worst: dismissing the episode as 'banter' and asking your colleague not to take it personally minimises the behaviour, tells her the team finds it acceptable and shifts the problem onto her.

B (3) takes the problem seriously but skips steps: you do not know what your colleague wants, and a first episode can often be resolved directly; it remains the right route if it happens again. A (2) does not make things worse in the short term, but silence leaves your colleague on her own and normalises the episode.
explanation.shortcut: On inclusion: support the person affected and address the behaviour; do not ignore it.
explanation.trap: A looks respectful because your colleague has not complained, but someone who has just joined rarely complains about a senior.
explanation.rule: Unacceptable behaviour must be addressed, with the most proportionate response that works.

items.stem: You are an analyst in an M&A team and have worked more than 90 hours a week for the past five weeks across two live deals. You have started making small mistakes, such as wrong cell references and typos in client pages, which your associate has caught. You feel exhausted and are sleeping about four hours a night. A third deal is about to start and the staffer asks whether you have capacity to join it. What should you do?
options: Tell the staffer honestly about your workload and the recent errors, and explain that you cannot take on a third deal now without quality slipping.
Accept the new deal to show commitment, and add an extra review pass on every piece of work across all three deals to catch mistakes before they reach the associate.
Accept the new deal, then quietly cut back the time you spend on the existing deals to make room for it.
Say you are at capacity, without giving details about your hours or the errors, and ask to be considered for the next deal instead.

steps: A is the best (resilience, communication): the staffer is asking precisely in order to allocate people well. Honest information on your workload and errors lets them decide and protects the quality of the deals in progress.
C is the worst: you accept a commitment you cannot honour and quietly reduce your attention on deals that are already live, with more errors and nobody aware of it.

D (3) protects you and the deals, but without context the staffer does not understand the urgency and does not know about the errors that have already emerged. B (2) looks like commitment, but adding work for someone who is making mistakes out of tiredness makes exactly that problem worse.
explanation.shortcut: If you are asked about your capacity, the right answer is honest and backed by facts.
explanation.trap: B looks like the 'banker' answer, but assessors reward those who manage their own capacity, not those who overload themselves.
explanation.rule: Flag your limits before they turn into errors in front of the client.

items.stem: You are a graduate in the settlements team of a global bank. At 3:20 pm you spot that a large bond trade due to settle today has a mismatch in the counterparty's account details; the settlement cut-off is 4 pm. Your supervisor, who normally handles these breaks, is on leave, and the team's escalation sheet names a senior analyst on the next desk as cover. You have seen this type of break fixed before. What should you do?
options: Correct the counterparty's account details in the system yourself, based on what you have seen done before, so the trade settles on time.
Flag the break at once to the senior analyst named as cover, with the trade details and time left to cut-off, and offer to help.
Email your supervisor, even though she is on leave, so that she can decide what to do when she next checks her messages.
Contact the counterparty directly to ask them to confirm their account details, and wait for their answer before telling anyone, so you do not raise a false alarm.

steps: B is the best (ownership, communication): you follow the designated escalation procedure, immediately give your colleague all the useful information and make yourself available. With 40 minutes to the cut-off, the speed of the handover is what counts.
A is the worst: changing a counterparty's account details on your own, without authorisation and verification, is a serious operational and fraud risk, even if you have seen it done before.

D (3) is a useful step towards resolving the discrepancy, but keeping it to yourself means that, if the reply arrives late, nobody can step in. C (2) involves the wrong person: they are on holiday, and the escalation sheet exists precisely for this.
explanation.shortcut: Urgent problem and the person responsible is away: use the designated backup immediately, with all the details.
explanation.trap: A looks like ownership, but in operations ownership means escalating properly, not making unauthorised changes.
explanation.rule: In operations, controls and the designated escalation route come before individual initiative.

items.stem: You are an analyst staffed on two deals. At 6 pm the VP on a sell-side mandate asks you to update the buyer list and teaser by 9 am tomorrow for an MD review. An hour later the VP on a live buy-side deal asks you to rerun the LBO model with new lender terms, also by 9 am, for a client call. Each task needs about six hours, and neither VP seems aware of the other request. What should you do?
options: Prioritise the LBO because it is for a client call, and tell the sell-side VP tonight that the buyer list may be delayed.
Work through the night to complete both tasks, without mentioning the clash to either VP, so that neither deadline is missed.
Tell both VPs about the clash tonight with your time estimates, suggest which task looks more urgent, and ask them to agree the priority.
Do the LBO first because it is for a client call, and email the sell-side VP at 8 am that the buyer list will be late.

steps: C is the best (prioritisation, communication): you make the conflict visible with data (6 + 6 hours in one night), give your proposal and let the people with authority decide. VPs would rather know at 19:00 than at 08:00.
D is the worst: you decide alone and warn the sell-side VP when there is no longer time to react before the review with the MD.

A (3) uses a reasonable criterion (client work first) and gives notice in time, but prioritising between two deals is not the analyst's call. B (2) looks like dedication, but 12 hours of work in one night puts the quality of both deliverables at risk and nobody knows there is a problem.
explanation.shortcut: Two seniors, one night: inform both immediately, make a proposal, let them decide.
explanation.trap: A is attractive because the 'client first' logic is correct, but it excludes the seniors from a decision that is theirs to make.
explanation.rule: Priority conflicts are made visible early, with estimates, and resolved by whoever has the authority.

items.stem: You and another first-year analyst are preparing a pitch book for a mid-cap industrial client, due to your associate on Thursday. You agreed to split the work: you do the valuation, he does the market and trading pages. It is Tuesday evening, he has delivered almost nothing and has been leaving early. You have already started covering some of his pages, and your own section is now at risk. The associate has not noticed. What should you do?
options: Keep doing his pages as well as your own, working late tonight and tomorrow, to make sure the pitch book reaches the associate on time.
At Wednesday's team check-in, point out in front of the associate that his pages are still not done.
Tell the associate that the timeline is at risk because the agreed work split is not working, and ask for guidance on next steps.
Speak to him privately tonight, ask whether something is getting in the way, and agree a plan for his pages with a Wednesday checkpoint.

steps: D is the best (teamwork, communication): you talk to him first, in private, because there may be a reason (another deal, a personal problem), and agree a plan that can be checked. If the plan falls through on Wednesday, you will have concrete facts with which to involve the associate.
B is the worst: exposing a colleague in front of the senior creates conflict, does not recover the pages and makes you look like an unreliable teammate.

C (3) is a legitimate, results-oriented escalation, but it skips the direct conversation with the colleague. A (2) may save the deadline, but it puts your own section at risk, does not address the cause and hides the problem from the associate.
explanation.shortcut: A colleague who is not contributing: first a direct conversation and a plan with checkpoints, then escalation if needed.
explanation.trap: A looks like team spirit, but silently covering for a structural problem lowers quality and postpones the conflict.
explanation.rule: Direct, private, concrete; escalation comes later, with the facts.

items.stem: You are an analyst on a sell-side mandate. Your MD is travelling and the associate is off sick. The client's CEO calls you directly, says his board meets tomorrow, and asks you to email him 'the valuation range you are working on', although it has not been reviewed by the MD or passed the bank's internal sign-off. He insists he only needs 'a rough number' and says he trusts you. What should you do?
options: Explain politely that you cannot share unreviewed figures, reach the MD straight away by phone or message, and tell the CEO when to expect an answer today.
Tell the CEO you will send the range once the MD has approved it, and email the MD asking him to look at the numbers when he can.
Tell the CEO that you are not able to help with this request and that he should contact the MD directly.
Email him the current draft range, clearly marked 'preliminary, subject to internal review', so that the board has something to work with.

steps: A is the best (client-focus, integrity): you protect the bank from unapproved numbers without leaving the client without an answer. You bring in the senior immediately and give the CEO a concrete timeline before the board.

D is the worst: a number in writing, even with a 'preliminary' disclaimer, becomes an anchor for the board and a risk for the bank if it later changes. Internal sign-off exists precisely for this reason.

B (3) respects the process, but a generic email to an MD who is travelling might not be read in time, and the client is left without a timeline. C (2) is right not to share, but it brushes the client off and comes across as unprofessional.
explanation.shortcut: A client request you cannot meet: no to the content, yes to the service (escalation and timeline).
explanation.trap: D looks like a smart compromise thanks to the disclaimer, but a number once sent can never be withdrawn.
explanation.rule: Never share unapproved output; always give the client a clear next step.

items.stem: You are an analyst in a coverage team. At 11 pm, reviewing the presentation for tomorrow's 9 am client board meeting, which your VP sent to the client this afternoon, you notice that the net debt on the valuation summary page excludes a EUR 40m lease liability. Including it lowers the implied equity value per share by about 3%. You built the page and the VP checked it. She is offline now but usually reads messages early. What should you do?
options: Say nothing, since the VP has already checked the page and a 3% difference is well within a typical valuation range anyway.
Wait until the morning and tell the VP in person before the meeting, so that you can walk her through the correction and its impact.
Message the VP tonight with a short explanation, the corrected page and the impact, so she can decide first thing how to handle it.
Email the corrected deck directly to the client tonight with a short note explaining the change, so that the board works from the right number.

steps: C is the best (integrity, ownership): you flag the error immediately, bring the corrected page and the quantified impact with you, and leave it to the VP to decide how to communicate it to the client before the board.
A is the worst: knowing that a number in front of the board is wrong and keeping quiet is a failure of integrity. The VP's review does not remove your responsibility for the page you built.

B (3) is transparent but slow: in the morning the VP would have very little time to decide. D (2) is honest but bypasses the hierarchy: the client relationship belongs to the VP, and an uncoordinated correction at 23:00 can cause confusion.
explanation.shortcut: Error discovered late: alert whoever owns the relationship immediately, with the correction and the impact already prepared.
explanation.trap: D looks the most transparent, but deciding how to communicate with the client is not the analyst's call.
explanation.rule: Flag early, bring the solution, leave the decision to whoever owns the relationship.

items.stem: You are a graduate on a rotation in the equities middle office. A senior trader, well liked and influential on the floor, asks you to amend the execution time on a trade ticket booked this morning, saying he 'fat-fingered the time' and that the real execution was 20 minutes earlier. The change would move the trade to before a market-moving company announcement. He says it is 'just admin' and needs it done before the end-of-day reports run. What should you do?
options: Ask him to confirm the correct execution time in an email so there is an audit trail, then make the change before the reports run.
Refuse to make the change and leave it there, since checking or investigating traders' bookings is not part of your role.
Make the change, since he executed the trade himself and is best placed to know exactly when it happened.
Tell him politely that you cannot amend execution times without evidence, and raise it with your supervisor under the trade amendment procedure.

steps: D is the best (integrity): moving a trade to before a price-sensitive announcement is a market abuse red flag. You refuse calmly and follow the amendment procedure with your supervisor, who can verify the time against objective evidence such as system logs.
C is the worst: amending without verification makes you party to a possible manipulation of records, and 'it's just admin' is not a justification.

B (3) avoids the immediate damage, but an attempt like this must be reported: staying silent leaves the risk open for the bank. A (2) creates a written record, but an email from the trader is not independent evidence and the amendment is still yours.
explanation.shortcut: Request to change a record close to a price-sensitive event: do not execute it, escalate according to procedure.
explanation.trap: A looks prudent because 'there is an email', but the confirmation comes from the very person who has the interest.
explanation.rule: Seniority and likeability do not change the rules on trading records.

items.stem: You are a junior analyst in an equity asset management team. Your portfolio manager asked for a two-page note on a mid-cap chemicals stock by 2 pm for the investment committee. At 12:30 you realise the consensus estimates you used come from a data export dated six weeks ago, before the company cut its guidance. Updating the numbers and the valuation would take about two hours. The PM is at her desk and reachable. What should you do?
options: Submit on time with a clear warning at the top that the estimates pre-date the guidance cut and that an updated version will follow.
Tell the PM now, offer an updated note at about 2:30 pm or an on-time version with a clear caveat, and start updating immediately.
Update the numbers and send the note about 30 minutes late without warning the PM, since accuracy matters more than timing for an investment committee.
Submit the note on time as it is, since the committee mainly focuses on the investment thesis rather than on the detailed estimates.

steps: B is the best (ownership, communication): you alert the PM 90 minutes ahead, offer two concrete options and start correcting straight away. The PM chooses knowing what is at stake.
D is the worst: presenting estimates you know are outdated after a guidance cut can lead the committee to a wrong investment decision.

A (3) is transparent and meets the deadline, but the committee still receives outdated numbers and the trade-off was chosen by you, not by the PM. C (2) produces correct work, but an uncommunicated delay may leave the committee without a note.
explanation.shortcut: Quality at risk close to a deadline: alert the person who commissioned the work immediately and propose options.
explanation.trap: C looks virtuous because it puts accuracy above everything, but the real mistake is staying silent about the delay.
explanation.rule: Never choose alone between quality and deadline: make the trade-off visible.

items.stem: You are a graduate analyst in market risk. This morning's report shows that the credit trading desk breached its daily VaR limit by 8%. When you call the desk to confirm the positions, the head trader says the breach is 'technical', caused by a hedge that will be booked by noon, and asks you to leave it out of the report you send to senior management so as not to 'create noise'. Your manager is in a meeting until 11 am. What should you do?
options: Include the breach in the report without the desk's explanation, and tell the trader firmly that what goes into the report is not negotiable.
Leave the breach out of the report as requested, since the hedge will be booked by noon and the breach is only technical.
Report the breach as required, adding the trader's explanation as context, and brief your manager as soon as her meeting ends.
Hold the report until noon to see whether the hedge is booked and the breach disappears, then send it with whatever the position shows.

steps: C is the best (integrity, communication): a breach is always reported, but including the desk's explanation makes the report more useful for management. Informing your manager as soon as she is free puts her in a position to handle any pressure.
B is the worst: omitting a breach at the request of the desk you are supposed to control is exactly the failure the risk function exists to prevent.

A (3) is right in substance, but without context the report is less informative and the tone risks damaging the relationship with the desk. D (2) looks prudent, but delaying a required report to see whether the problem goes away is still a way of hiding it.
explanation.shortcut: In risk and compliance, numbers are reported as they are: context is added to the data, it does not replace it.
explanation.trap: D looks like a reasonable compromise, but selective delay is a form of omission.
explanation.rule: Independence of control: report everything, with context, and involve your manager.

items.stem: It is Monday morning. You are an analyst with three requests due on Wednesday evening: a comparable companies analysis for an MD's pitch (about 9 hours), a data room index for a live sell-side deal (about 7 hours) and industry research for a VP's internal training session (about 6 hours). Your recurring daily tasks need another 12 hours over the three days, and you can realistically work about 30 hours in that time. What should you do?
options: Ask a fellow analyst from another team to prepare the data room index, without telling the deal team, so you can focus on the rest.
Work through the requests in the order they arrived, staying late each evening as needed to get as much done as possible.
Do the live deal and the pitch first, and quietly produce a lighter version of the training research without telling the VP who asked for it.
Map out the hours, tell the requesters today that you are about four hours short, and propose rescoping or delaying the training research.

steps: D is the best (prioritisation, communication): you quantify the problem (9 + 7 + 6 + 12 = 34 hours of work against 30 available, a gap of 4 hours), flag it immediately and propose sacrificing the least critical task, namely the research for an internal training session.
A is the worst: handing a deliverable for a live deal to someone outside the team, without telling anyone, creates a confidentiality and quality risk that the deal team knows nothing about.

C (3) has the right priorities (live deal and pitch first), but quietly cutting back the work for the VP takes away their chance to decide or find an alternative. B (2) does not prioritise at all: order of arrival does not reflect importance, and the 4-hour gap remains.
explanation.shortcut: Workload above capacity: do the maths, communicate the gap immediately, propose what to cut.
explanation.trap: C looks pragmatic, but a cut not communicated to the requester is a guaranteed nasty surprise.
explanation.rule: Prioritise by impact and urgency, and negotiate cuts openly.

items.stem: You are on the second of four rotations in a bank's graduate programme, currently in the trade finance operations team. You had hoped for a front-office placement and find the work repetitive. Your rotation manager is supportive but busy, and your end-of-rotation review, which counts towards your final placement, is in three months. A friend in the M&A team tells you there may be an opening there for your next rotation. What should you do?
options: Commit fully to the rotation, ask your manager for a stretching project, and build relationships with the M&A team in your own time.
Ask your rotation manager to move you to M&A straight away, explaining honestly that operations is not where you see your long-term career.
Keep doing your work well, but say nothing about your interest in M&A until the end-of-rotation review, so as not to seem distracted.
Do the minimum required in your current team and put most of your energy into networking with the M&A team for your next rotation.

steps: A is the best (resilience, ownership): you give your best where you are, because the review matters and trade finance teaches you a lot about companies' real flows. In parallel you build your path towards M&A without taking energy away from the work.
D is the worst: disengagement is noticed immediately, worsens the review that decides your final placement, and reputations within the programme travel between teams, M&A included.

C (3) maintains a good standard of work, but not letting anyone know what interests you reduces your chances. B (2) is honest, but asking to leave mid-rotation signals little resilience and is rarely possible.
explanation.shortcut: A rotation you do not enjoy: excel where you are and build the next step in parallel.
explanation.trap: B looks proactive and transparent, but on graduate programmes switching mid-rotation is read as a lack of commitment.
explanation.rule: Reputation is built in every rotation, not only in the one you prefer.

items.stem: You work in the equity capital markets team. In a crowded lift in your office building, which is shared with other companies, you hear two colleagues from another team of your bank openly discussing the timing of a client's upcoming share placement, mentioning the client's name. The placement has not been announced. You know the two colleagues only by sight, and several people in the lift do not work for the bank. What should you do?
options: Say nothing in the lift, then find a discreet moment afterwards to remind them that the building is shared with other companies.
Discreetly interrupt them, for example by suggesting they pick it up upstairs, then speak to them afterwards and tell compliance what happened.
Say nothing, since they are not in your team, you barely know them and what they discuss is not your responsibility.
Tell them clearly and loudly enough to stop them at once that they should not be discussing confidential client matters in a shared lift.

steps: B is the best (integrity): you stop the information leak as it happens, without drawing attention, and then involve compliance, because the client's name and the timing of an unannounced placement may already have got out.
C is the worst: this is inside information on an unannounced transaction, overheard by outsiders. Confidentiality is everyone's responsibility at the bank, not just the deal team's.

A (3) has the right tone, but lets the conversation continue and does not consider whether the incident should be reported. D (2) stops the conversation but, by saying out loud that it is 'confidential', confirms to the outsiders that the information is sensitive and embarrasses your colleagues.
explanation.shortcut: Information leak in progress: stop it immediately and discreetly, then consider reporting it.
explanation.trap: C looks respectful of the boundaries between teams, but with inside information there is no such thing as 'it's none of my business'.
explanation.rule: Confidentiality is defended immediately and discreetly, and reported when there is a real risk.

items.stem: You are an analyst in a leveraged finance team. Rushing before a call, you email a draft term sheet containing the client's confidential financial projections to the wrong external address: autocomplete picked a contact at another company with a similar name. You notice two minutes later and the email has not bounced. Your VP is on the call you are about to join, which will last an hour. What should you do?
options: Email the wrong recipient asking them to delete the message, and tell your VP after the call.
Try to recall the email and, if the recall appears to work, say nothing to avoid embarrassment.
Join the call and report the incident to your VP and compliance at the end of the day, once your other tasks are done.
Attempt a recall, message your VP immediately, and report the incident to compliance or the data protection team following the bank's procedure.

steps: D is the best (integrity, ownership): you admit the mistake at once, try to contain it and trigger the incident procedure. With a client's confidential data every minute counts, and the bank may have notification obligations with strict deadlines.
B is the worst: a recall that 'appears' to have worked is no guarantee, and hiding a possible breach of client data turns a mistake into an integrity problem.

A (3) tries to limit the damage and informs the VP, but skips the formal procedure and leaves you handling a sensitive external contact on your own. C (2) is honest, but a delay of hours reduces the chance of containing the spread.
explanation.shortcut: Mistake involving confidential data: contain it, report it immediately, follow the incident procedure.
explanation.trap: A looks responsible, but handling the relationship with an external third party on your own is no substitute for formal reporting.
explanation.rule: Mistakes are declared immediately: hiding them is always worse than the mistake itself.

items.stem: You work in a hybrid credit research team and share coverage of European telecoms with a peer who joined three months ago. Over the past few weeks she has stopped turning her camera on, replies to messages hours later and has missed two internal deadlines, which you covered. On your last call she sounded flat and said she was 'just tired'. Your manager has not said anything about it. What should you do?
options: Arrange an informal one-to-one to ask how she is doing, listen without judging, and point her to the support the firm offers.
Tell your manager that you are worried about her, sharing the two missed deadlines you have covered and the other changes you have noticed.
Post in the team chat asking whether everyone is okay, since some people in the team seem less engaged lately.
Respect her privacy and keep covering her deadlines without saying anything, since she has told you she is just tired.

steps: A is the best (teamwork, communication): a private, informal check-in is the least intrusive way to find out whether there is a problem and to point her towards the right support. You do not have to solve it yourself, but you can be the first to notice.
C is the worst: a generic message in the team channel is passive-aggressive, embarrasses your colleague and opens no real dialogue.

B (3) is legitimate if the concern persists, because team wellbeing is the manager's responsibility, but it is better to speak to her directly first. D (2) is kind in the short term, but silently covering her deadlines does not address the cause and is not sustainable.
explanation.shortcut: Colleague who is struggling: private check-in, listen, point her to the support available.
explanation.trap: D seems to respect her privacy, but silence leaves the person on her own and hides the problem from the team.
explanation.rule: On other people's wellbeing: notice, ask privately, signpost; do not judge and do not ignore.

items.stem: You are an analyst in a corporate banking team. The CFO of a mid-sized client emails you directly, copying no one, asking you to send a revised term sheet for a EUR 150m revolving credit facility with the margin reduced by 25 basis points, 'as agreed verbally with your relationship manager last week'. You have no record of this agreement, and the relationship manager is on a flight to New York for the next eight hours. The CFO wants the document today. What should you do?
options: Prepare the revised term sheet and send it to the relationship manager for approval when he lands, without replying to the CFO for now, so you do not commit to anything.
Reply that you are unable to help with the term sheet and that he should wait for the relationship manager to land in New York.
Reply to the CFO that you need to confirm the terms internally, tell him when to expect an answer, then contact a senior colleague on the deal and the relationship manager.
Send the revised term sheet as requested, since the CFO says the change was agreed with the relationship manager and wants it today.

steps: C is the best (client-focus, integrity): you reply to the client immediately with a concrete timeline, but you do not change economic terms without confirmation. Also involving an available senior colleague avoids everything being blocked for eight hours.

D is the worst: 25 bps on EUR 150m is worth up to EUR 375k a year if the facility is fully drawn, and you have no evidence of the agreement. Sending amended terms on the client's word alone exposes the bank.

A (3) is proactive and respects the approval process, but leaves the CFO without a reply for hours. B (2) is right in substance but blunt and passive: the client does not know when he will receive an answer.
explanation.shortcut: Request on unverified economic terms: reply to the client immediately, confirm internally before changing anything.
explanation.trap: A looks efficient because the document is ready, but silence towards the client comes at a cost to the relationship.
explanation.rule: Never change economic terms without internal confirmation; never leave a client without a reply.

items.stem: You are an analyst in a financial sponsors coverage team. Your associate built the LBO template that the whole team uses. While working on your third model with it, you notice that taxes are calculated on EBIT instead of pre-tax profit, so interest is never tax-deductible and cash available for debt repayment is understated in every model built on it. Two live models currently use the template. The associate is proud of it and can react badly to criticism. What should you do?
options: Fix the formula in your own model only and leave the template as it is, to avoid an awkward conversation with the associate.
Raise it privately with the associate, show the formula and its impact on a live model, and offer to fix the template and both live models.
Raise the issue at next week's team meeting so that everyone using the template hears about it at the same time and can update their models.
Email the VP about the issue straight away, since it affects two live deals and the associate is likely to react defensively if you raise it with him.

steps: B is the best (communication, ownership): you raise the issue first with the person who built the template, privately and with concrete evidence, and you immediately offer the fix. Even a touchy associate finds it easier to accept a problem presented with the correction already prepared.
A is the worst: you know that two live models understate the cash available to repay debt and you choose to keep quiet to avoid embarrassment. It is a risk for the clients and for the bank.

D (3) ensures the problem gets fixed, but going over the associate's head without speaking to him damages trust within the team. C (2) is neutral in tone, but waiting for the weekly meeting leaves the live models wrong for longer and exposes the associate in front of everyone.
explanation.shortcut: Error in a senior's work: raise it privately, with evidence and a fix, and quickly if it affects live deals.
explanation.trap: D seems prudent because it involves the VP, but bypassing the person directly concerned is a shortcut that costs trust.
explanation.rule: Upward feedback: private, factual, with a solution in hand.

items.stem: You are presenting your individual case study to two assessors at a bank's assessment centre. Halfway through, while explaining your recommendation that the client should fund an expansion with a new bank loan, you realise you misread the interest coverage ratio in the pack: it is 1.8x, not 3.8x. At 1.8x, taking on more debt looks considerably riskier. You have about five minutes left, and both assessors have the full pack in front of them. What should you do?
options: Finish the presentation as prepared to keep your structure and timing, and mention the error briefly at the end if there is time.
Acknowledge the error and tell the assessors that you would need more time with the numbers before you could revisit your recommendation.
Continue with your original recommendation, since changing your view in the middle of the presentation would make you look indecisive.
Acknowledge the error openly, explain how the lower coverage changes the risk, and adjust your recommendation, for example to a smaller loan.

steps: D is the best (integrity, resilience): correcting yourself openly and adapting the recommendation in real time demonstrates what assessors are looking for, namely judgement, honesty and clear thinking under pressure.
C is the worst: defending a recommendation based on a number you know is wrong is an integrity problem, and the assessors almost certainly have the correct figure in front of them.

B (3) is honest, but stops halfway: in five minutes you can at least say in which direction the recommendation changes. A (2) postpones the correction and leaves the assessors listening to an argument you know is weak.
explanation.shortcut: Mistake discovered while presenting: admit it, explain the impact, update the conclusion.
explanation.trap: A looks like an elegant compromise, but every minute spent on a flawed analysis weighs on your assessment.
explanation.rule: Correcting a mistake in public is worth more than a presentation that is perfect only on the surface.

items.stem: You are a graduate in a fund administration operations team. Every morning the team spends about two hours manually reconciling cash balances across 40 funds in spreadsheets. In your own time you have built a simple macro that cuts this to 20 minutes on test data. When you mention it, your manager says the current process 'has worked for years' and that she does not want to risk errors in the reconciliations. What should you do?
options: Propose a few weeks' parallel run, checking the macro's results against the manual process, and offer to have it documented and reviewed by controls.
Start using the macro anyway for your share of the reconciliation, since it is faster and you have already tested it on sample data.
Accept the decision for now, keep improving the macro in your own time and raise the idea again at your next one-to-one with more evidence.
Ask a senior colleague from another team, who already uses similar tools, to persuade your manager that the macro is a good idea.

steps: A is the best (ownership, communication): you respond to the manager's specific concern, the risk of errors, with a parallel run that measures it, and you involve controls. The decision is then based on data, not opinions.
B is the worst: using an unvalidated tool in a reconciliation, against the manager's decision, creates precisely the operational risk she feared and undermines trust.

C (3) respects the manager and keeps the idea alive, but postpones it without addressing her objection. D (2) tries to persuade her by going around her: even if the idea is good, the manager will feel bypassed.
explanation.shortcut: Idea rejected because of risk: propose a controlled, low-risk way to trial it and measure it.
explanation.trap: C seems patient and respectful, but gives the manager nothing new that might change her mind.
explanation.rule: To get a change accepted, answer the real objection with a controlled test.

items.stem: You are an analyst travelling by train to a client meeting with your associate, who is sitting in another carriage. You need to finish updating the merger model before the meeting in 90 minutes. The train is crowded, the passenger next to you can easily see your screen, and you do not have a privacy filter. The model shows both companies' names, and the deal has not been announced. What should you do?
options: Carry on working normally, since the passenger is unlikely to understand a financial model and you need every minute before the meeting.
Keep working on the model as planned, but hide the company names and rename the tabs while you are on the train so nothing identifies the deal.
Move to a seat where your screen cannot be seen or, failing that, work only on non-sensitive parts and agree a plan with your associate.
Stop working on the model completely and tell your associate that you will finish the update at the client site, just before the meeting starts.

steps: C is the best (integrity, prioritisation): first you protect confidentiality by finding a safe spot, then you reorganise your work around non-sensitive parts and agree a realistic plan for the meeting with the associate.
A is the worst: an unannounced deal with the companies' names on a visible screen is a potential leak of inside information, and you do not know who the passenger next to you is.

D (3) fully protects the deal and informs the associate, but gives up too early on working on non-sensitive parts. B (2) only partly reduces the risk: numbers, sector and structure may be enough to identify the companies.
explanation.shortcut: In public, confidentiality beats convenience: change your setting or change your task, and warn whoever depends on you.
explanation.trap: B looks like a clever technical fix, but hiding the names does not make an M&A model anonymous.
explanation.rule: Never work on confidential material where others can see or hear it.

items.stem: You are an analyst in a debt capital markets team. In a team meeting, a junior colleague, Elena, suggests pricing a client's new bond against a different peer group. Nobody reacts. Ten minutes later, a male associate makes almost the same suggestion and the director praises it as 'a great insight'. You have seen this happen to Elena before, and once again she says nothing. The meeting is still going on. What should you do?
options: Say nothing, since the idea is being used and the outcome for the client is the same.
In the meeting, say something like 'that builds on Elena's point earlier', so that her contribution is acknowledged.
After the meeting, tell Elena you noticed what happened and ask whether she would like support in raising it.
After the meeting, tell the associate in front of other colleagues that he took credit for Elena's idea.

steps: B is the best (teamwork, integrity): a neutral, immediate acknowledgement corrects the attribution without accusing anyone and is almost impossible to dispute. The director understands where the idea came from.
D is the worst: accusing the associate in front of others creates open conflict, puts Elena at the centre of a scene she did not ask for and is unlikely to change behaviour.
C (3) is respectful and helpful, especially because this keeps happening, but it comes when the credit has already been given. A (2) ignores a pattern that harms your colleague and the team climate.
explanation.shortcut: Unattributed idea: restore the credit in the moment itself, in a neutral way.
explanation.trap: D seems brave and fair, but a public confrontation shifts the focus to the conflict rather than the idea.
explanation.rule: Inclusion is practised in real time, with simple, non-confrontational gestures.

items.stem: You are a junior client service analyst at an asset manager. A pension fund client calls, clearly angry: their multi-asset portfolio underperformed its benchmark by 3.2 percentage points last quarter, and he says he learned this from the quarterly report rather than from the firm. He demands to speak to the portfolio manager immediately and mentions reviewing the mandate. The portfolio manager is presenting at an investor conference until 4 pm. What should you do?
options: Listen and acknowledge his frustration, then book a call with the portfolio manager after 4 pm today, confirm it by email and brief the PM beforehand.
Message the portfolio manager at the conference and ask him to step out of his session and call the client back straight away, as the mandate is at risk.
Explain that markets were difficult for everyone last quarter and reassure him that the underperformance is likely to reverse over the coming months.
Tell him the portfolio manager is at a conference today and will call him back at some point later this week.

steps: A is the best (client-focus, resilience): first you listen and acknowledge the problem, then you make a concrete commitment (a call with the PM today) and confirm it in writing. The briefing prepares the PM for a conversation on which the mandate depends.
C is the worst: playing it down with 'it was difficult for everyone' sounds defensive, and predicting a recovery in performance is a promise you cannot make.

B (3) shows urgency, but pulling the PM out of a presentation without context leads to an improvised, unprepared call. D (2) is factually correct but vague: for a client who is talking about reviewing the mandate, 'later this week' is not enough.
explanation.shortcut: Angry client: listen, acknowledge, make a concrete commitment with a time, confirm it in writing.
explanation.trap: B looks the most client-focused, but responsiveness without preparation can make the conversation worse.
explanation.rule: With a dissatisfied client, a precise commitment is worth more than an immediate response.

items.stem: You are a second-year analyst supervising a summer intern on a sell-side deal. You asked him to build a trading comparables table. He delivered it on time, but several multiples mix calendar-year and fiscal-year figures, and two of the peers are not really comparable. The intern is enthusiastic and has received little feedback so far. The associate needs the table by tomorrow afternoon, and you have a couple of hours free this evening. What should you do?
options: Fix the table yourself tonight using your free hours to make sure it is right, and thank the intern for delivering his work on time.
Tell the associate that the intern's work was not good enough and ask whether a different intern could be assigned to the deal instead.
Go through the issues with the intern in person, explain why they matter, and ask him to fix them by tomorrow morning so you can review the table.
Send the intern a detailed list of the errors by email this evening and ask him to correct them all before the associate needs the table tomorrow afternoon.

steps: C is the best (communication, teamwork): specific, explained feedback teaches the intern why multiples must be calculated on consistent periods and how to choose a peer. The deadline leaves time both for the corrections and for your review.
B is the worst: you offload the problem onto the associate instead of exercising the supervision you were entrusted with, and the intern learns nothing.

D (3) flags the errors but without explaining them: the intern might correct them without understanding them and then repeat them. A (2) guarantees the result, but the intern does not know he made mistakes and you take on work that helps nobody grow.
explanation.shortcut: Errors by a junior you supervise: specific, explained feedback, with time to correct them.
explanation.trap: A looks the safest for quality, but giving up on feedback is a failure as a supervisor.
explanation.rule: Useful feedback is specific, timely and explains why.

items.stem: You are an analyst preparing valuation pages for a sell-side pitch. Your MD asks you to remove one listed peer from the trading comparables because its 6.0x EV/EBITDA multiple 'drags the range down', lowering the indicative valuation you can show the client. The peer operates in the same niche with similar size and margins, but it recently lost a large customer and faces a pending lawsuit. The other six peers trade between 8.5x and 10.5x. What should you do?
options: Tell the MD you are uncomfortable removing a peer that is so similar in size and margins, and ask him to reconsider his request before the pitch.
Suggest excluding the peer for its company-specific issues, disclosed on the page with the reason, and show the MD the range with and without it.
Remove the peer as instructed without further comment, since the MD is responsible for the valuation and knows the client best.
Keep the peer in the table without telling the MD, since you believe including all the comparable companies is the more accurate approach.

steps: B is the best (integrity, communication): there is a legitimate reason to exclude the peer (loss of a large customer, litigation), but only if it is disclosed. Showing the range with and without it gives the MD what he is asking for and keeps the page defensible in front of the client.
D is the worst: silently ignoring an MD's instruction on a judgement call creates a surprise, probably in front of the client, and burns trust without explaining anything.

A (3) raises the issue correctly, but overlooks the fact that the exclusion has a reasonable basis and proposes no solution. C (2) respects the hierarchy, but an undisclosed removal makes the selection of comparables less transparent and easier to challenge.
explanation.shortcut: Questionable but defensible judgement call: make it transparent and show the alternatives.
explanation.trap: At the harder levels 'integrity' does not mean opposing everything: excluding an outlier with specific issues is standard practice, hiding it is not.
explanation.rule: Valuation choices can be debated; undisclosed ones cannot.

items.stem: You are a graduate in a bank's equity research team. You receive an email clearly intended for someone in the M&A team with a similar name. The preview shows it concerns a heavily discounted rights issue that a listed retailer is preparing with the bank, not yet announced. You hold a small number of shares in that retailer in a personal account, bought last year and declared to compliance, and you were already planning to sell them this week. What should you do?
options: Sell the shares as planned this week, since you had decided to sell them before you received the email and they are already declared.
Forward the email to the intended recipient in the M&A team so that it reaches the right person, then delete it from your inbox.
Delete the email without reading further, tell the sender it was misdirected, and postpone the sale of your shares until the rights issue is public.
Stop reading, tell compliance at once that you received the email and hold shares in the company, and do not trade until they clear you.

steps: D is the best (integrity): you now hold inside information and you work on the 'public' side of the Chinese wall. Compliance must know immediately, both because of your personal account and because of any restrictions on research work on the stock.

A is the worst: selling now, ahead of non-public negative news, means avoiding a loss thanks to inside information. It is insider dealing even if the intention came earlier: an idea to sell is not an order already placed.

C (3) avoids the trade and limits the spread, but without compliance the bank does not know the wall has been crossed. B (2) gets the email to the right person, but spreads the information further and addresses neither the reporting nor the conflict with your shares.
explanation.shortcut: Inside information received by mistake: stop reading, do not trade, call compliance.
explanation.trap: A seems defensible because 'I had already decided', but under market abuse rules what matters is what you know at the moment you trade.
explanation.rule: With inside information: stop reading, stop trading, report to compliance.

items.stem: You are an analyst attending a client board meeting with your VP in 30 minutes. She is driving to the client's offices and not answering calls. Doing a final check of the printed packs you are bringing, you notice that the share count on the valuation page omits the shares issued in last month's placing, so equity value per share is overstated by about 6%. Your MD is on the deal team but not attending, and you can reach him. What should you do?
options: Call the MD, explain the issue and its impact and, with his agreement, prepare a corrected page, sending the VP a short summary to read on arrival.
Reprint the page with the corrected figure and swap it into the packs without telling anyone, since the correction is clearly right.
Leave the packs as they are and tell the VP after the meeting, since there is no time left to fix the page properly.
Keep trying to call the VP while she drives and tell her about the error as soon as she arrives, so that she can decide how to handle it.

steps: A is the best (ownership, communication): you involve the only senior you can reach, bring the quantified impact and a ready solution, and inform the VP in writing so she can read it as soon as she arrives. The decision stays with a senior, but no time is lost.
C is the worst: knowingly presenting a board with a value per share overstated by 6% is a serious reputational risk and an integrity problem.

D (3) is transparent and respects the person presenting, but leaves the VP with no time to decide and no correction ready. B (2) puts the right number in front of the board, but an unagreed change surprises the VP, who could find herself commenting on numbers different from the ones she knows.
explanation.shortcut: Critical error, person in charge unreachable, little time: alternative senior, correction ready, written record.
explanation.trap: B looks like ownership at its best, but an unagreed change to board materials creates a new risk.
explanation.rule: When time is short, speed up the escalation: do not skip it.

items.stem: You are a graduate in a corporate banking team. A fellow graduate, who is also a close friend, mentions that he regularly forwards client spreadsheets to his personal email so he can work on his own laptop at weekends, because remote access is slow. You know the bank's policy forbids sending client data to personal accounts. He says 'everyone does it' and asks you not to make a big deal of it. What should you do?
options: Ask him how he sets it up, since sending files home would also help you get through your own weekend work more easily.
Report the situation to compliance straight away without discussing it with him any further, since client data is involved and the bank may need to act on it quickly.
Tell him that it is risky and could get him into trouble, but leave it to him to decide what to do since he is a friend.
Tell him it breaches policy, urge him to delete the files and self-report to IT security today, and say you will report it if he does not.

steps: D is the best (integrity, teamwork): you are clear about the risk and give your friend the chance to put it right and self-report, which is the least damaging route for him, but you set a precise limit: if he does not do it today, you will report it.
A is the worst: instead of stopping the breach you replicate it, increasing the risk to client data and becoming jointly responsible for it.

B (3) protects the bank and its clients, but gives up on getting your colleague to correct his behaviour in a more constructive and equally quick way. C (2) names the risk, but leaving everything to his discretion means the data almost certainly stays on his laptop.
explanation.shortcut: Colleague breaching a security policy: talk to him directly, ask him to self-report by a deadline, escalate if he does not act.
explanation.trap: B looks the most principled, but at the harder levels the best answer combines integrity and collaboration rather than setting them against each other.
explanation.rule: Friendship and loyalty do not extend to covering up risks to client data.

items.stem: You are an analyst in a coverage team. A client whose bond issue your bank is currently arranging invites you and your associate to the final of a major tennis tournament in its corporate box, with dinner included. Tickets like these are worth several hundred euros each. Your associate says the relationship matters and suggests you both go. Bank policy allows client entertainment within limits if pre-approved, and requires extra scrutiny during live transactions. What should you do?
options: Accept and attend with your associate, then record the event in the gifts and entertainment register the following week.
Decline politely for yourself, telling the client that you cannot attend hospitality events while a transaction with the bank is live.
Suggest to your associate that you both seek pre-approval from compliance before replying, and accept only if it is approved.
Accept and attend without recording it anywhere, since a relationship event with a client is not the same as receiving a gift.

steps: C is the best (integrity, client-focus): the policy allows entertainment with pre-approval, and scrutiny is stricter during a live deal. Asking compliance first protects both the client relationship and the bank, whatever the outcome.
D is the worst: a valuable event offered by a client with a transaction in progress is exactly what the policy wants to track. Not recording it is a breach, whatever you call it.

B (3) removes the risk, but gives up a potentially legitimate relationship opportunity without going through the process, and makes a different decision from the associate. A (2) declares the event, but after the fact: the policy requires approval beforehand, precisely because there is a live deal.
explanation.shortcut: Entertainment offered by a client: the best answer is 'pre-approval', not an automatic yes or no.
explanation.trap: B looks the most ethical, but at the harder levels the best choice follows the process rather than avoiding the situation altogether.
explanation.rule: Approval first, then acceptance: never declare only after the event.

items.stem: You are a graduate in the product control team. It is 7 pm on month-end, and your manager asks you to sign off the daily P&L reconciliation for a trading desk so the numbers can go to the CFO's office by 8 pm. You have reconciled every position except one, which shows an unexplained difference of EUR 1.2m that you have not yet investigated. Your manager says it is 'probably a timing issue' and that you can check it tomorrow. What should you do?
options: Spend the next 40 minutes investigating the difference yourself and sign off if it turns out to be a timing issue, telling your manager this is your plan.
Explain that you cannot confirm a reconciliation with an unexplained EUR 1.2m difference, and propose sending the numbers by 8 pm with it flagged as an open item.
Sign off as asked, since your manager is more experienced, believes it is a timing issue and has taken responsibility for the decision.
Refuse to sign off and tell your manager that the numbers cannot go to the CFO's office until you have fully investigated the difference.

steps: B is the best (integrity, communication): you do not sign off what you cannot confirm, but you do not block the process either. Sending the numbers by 8 pm with the difference flagged as an open item gives the CFO's office true and complete information.

C is the worst: the sign-off certifies that the reconciliation is complete. Signing off with EUR 1.2m unexplained because it is 'probably' a timing issue is a false attestation, and the responsibility remains yours.

A (3) is proactive and might solve the problem, but if the analysis is not closed by 8 pm you face the same choice with less time. D (2) defends the integrity of the control, but without alternatives the report is missed and the relationship with the manager becomes strained.
explanation.shortcut: Pressure to sign off something incomplete: do not sign, propose sending it with the exception disclosed.
explanation.trap: A looks like the ideal middle way, but it ties your sign-off to the hope of finding the explanation in time.
explanation.rule: A sign-off certifies a fact: sign off only what you have verified, and disclose the rest as an exception.

items.stem: You are in the first year of a bank's graduate programme, placed in a corporate banking team. The graduate programme office has scheduled a mandatory two-day regulatory training on Thursday and Friday; missing it means repeating the whole module later. On Tuesday your team director asks you to stay on a client refinancing that needs a credit paper finalised by Friday noon, saying 'training can wait'. You are the only analyst on the deal. What should you do?
options: Tell the director what missing the training would mean, offer to finish most of the paper by Wednesday with a handover note, and ask him to settle it with the programme office.
Skip the training without telling the graduate programme office, since the director has asked you to stay and the client deadline is more important.
Contact the graduate programme office yourself and ask them to exempt you from this week's training, explaining the client deadline and that you are the only analyst working on the deal.
Attend the training as scheduled and leave the director to find someone else to finish the credit paper while you are away on Thursday and Friday.

steps: A is the best (prioritisation, communication): the director may not know the consequences of missing the mandatory training. You give him the facts, bring work forward to reduce the risk to the deal and pass the decision to the two people who have the authority to make it.
B is the worst: skipping mandatory regulatory training without saying so breaches the programme rules and exposes you personally; 'the director asked me to' does not protect you.

C (3) looks for a solution through the right channel, but without coordinating with the director you risk receiving two incompatible answers. D (2) meets the formal obligation, but leaves a deal without an analyst and without a handover plan.
explanation.shortcut: Conflict between two authorities: inform, reduce the risk by working ahead, get the authorities to talk to each other.
explanation.trap: B looks like the team choice because it puts the client first, but it ignores a regulatory obligation.
explanation.rule: When two seniors ask for incompatible things, your job is to make the conflict visible and propose a plan.

items.stem: You are an analyst in a leveraged finance team. A lateral hire who joined last week from a competitor bank shares with you, in a friendly way, a folder of 'useful templates', including a lender presentation with the competitor's internal pricing grid and a client's financial projections. She says it will save you hours on your current pitch, which targets the same client. Your pitch is due in two days and you are behind. What should you do?
options: Use only the formatting and slide structure of her templates to save time on the pitch, and ignore the client data and the competitor's pricing grid.
Use the pricing grid and the projections, since they would make your pitch far more competitive against her former bank.
Do not use the material, tell her it is likely to be confidential to her former employer and its client, and inform your associate or compliance.
Do not use any of the material and quietly delete it from your folders, without saying anything to her so as not to embarrass a new colleague.

steps: C is the best (integrity, teamwork): the material contains confidential information belonging to another bank and to a client. You do not use it, you help your colleague understand the risk and you involve the people who can handle it properly, which also protects her.
B is the worst: using a competitor's confidential pricing grid and a client's projections to win a pitch exposes you and the bank to breaches of confidentiality and to legal consequences.

D (3) avoids using the material, but your colleague might share it with others and the bank remains exposed. A (2) looks like a compromise, but you still use material that should never have entered the bank and you do not solve the problem.
explanation.shortcut: Confidential information from a former employer: do not use it, do not stay silent, involve those who manage the risk.
explanation.trap: A seems harmless because 'it is just formatting', but the problem is that the material is in the bank at all, not how much of it you use.
explanation.rule: Competitive advantage can never come from other people's confidential information.

items.stem: You are an analyst in an M&A team. Your sister's wedding is on Saturday in another city; you booked the time off two months ago and your staffer approved it. On Friday at 3 pm, the VP on a live deal tells you that the buyer has moved the bid deadline forward and the team will need to work all weekend on the model and the bid letter. He asks whether you can 'make it work'. What should you do?
options: Cancel your plans for the wedding and work the whole weekend with the team, since a live deal with a new bid deadline has to come first.
Explain your long-standing commitment, offer to work late tonight and all of Sunday, and leave a clear handover for Saturday while staying reachable for urgent questions.
Remind the VP that your leave was approved two months ago and go to the wedding without offering any further help to the team.
Agree to work all weekend, then attend the wedding anyway and reply to the team's messages whenever you get the chance.

steps: B is the best (communication, teamwork, resilience): you honour a personal commitment approved long ago but take responsibility for your share of the work with concrete proposals. The VP can plan the weekend knowing exactly when you are available.
D is the worst: you promise availability you know you cannot guarantee, and the team discovers the problem at the worst possible moment.

A (3) guarantees cover for the deal, but you give up a once-in-a-lifetime event when a middle-ground solution exists, and it is not a sustainable model. C (2) is formally correct, but on a live deal offering no help at all leaves the team struggling and damages trust.
explanation.shortcut: Important personal commitment versus urgent work: do not pick an extreme, negotiate a concrete solution.
explanation.trap: A looks like the answer a bank 'wants', but modern tests reward people who manage their own limits transparently and constructively.
explanation.rule: Be transparent about your commitments, make concrete proposals on the work, and never promise what you cannot deliver.

items.stem: You are an analyst drafting the information memorandum for a sell-side process. The client's management has provided an 'adjusted EBITDA' of EUR 48m for last year, which they want as the headline figure. Reconciling it with the audited accounts, you find reported EBITDA of EUR 41m plus EUR 7m of add-backs, of which EUR 4m are 'one-off' restructuring costs that have recurred in each of the last three years. Your VP says management is the client and 'adjusted figures are standard'. What should you do?
options: Replace the headline with the EUR 41m audited EBITDA and email management directly, telling them that their adjusted figure is misleading.
Raise the issue with the VP and, if he still wants the EUR 48m headline, ask compliance to review the memorandum before it goes out to buyers.
Use the EUR 48m as instructed without raising the point, since adjusted EBITDA is common practice and management owns the numbers in the memorandum.
Show the VP your reconciliation, highlight the recurring EUR 4m, and suggest showing a clear bridge from audited to adjusted EBITDA for him to discuss with management.

steps: D is the best (integrity, client-focus): you do not challenge adjusted EBITDA as such, which is standard practice, but you point out that EUR 4m of costs that recurred in three years out of three can hardly be considered 'one-off'. A transparent bridge from EUR 41m to EUR 48m protects both the client in due diligence and the bank.

A is the worst: you go over the VP's head and challenge management, that is the client, in writing, taking away from the person who manages the relationship the chance to deal with the issue. The concern is well founded, but the approach creates needless conflict and damages the mandate.

B (3) raises the issue and allows for an escalation, but goes to compliance before proposing a solution the VP might accept. C (2) follows the instruction without raising the point: at a hypothetical multiple of 8x, that EUR 4m of EBITDA is worth about EUR 32m of enterprise value, buyers will discover it in the quality of earnings review and the credibility of the process will suffer.
explanation.shortcut: Questionable client figure: do not accept it and do not replace it on your own; make it transparent with a reconciliation.
explanation.trap: A looks the most principled choice because it uses the audited figure, but the approach, unilateral and confrontational towards the client, makes it the worst.
explanation.rule: Transparency through reconciliation; the decision rests with whoever has the authority.
